title: Interfaces vs Abstract Classes
summary: Contract-only vs partial implementation, and how modern languages blurred the line with default methods — plus the fat-interface pitfall and marker interfaces.

slides.markdown:
An **interface** is pure contract — method signatures, no implementation (traditionally). An **abstract class** can mix contract with partial, shared implementation. Both are abstraction mechanisms, but they solve for different situations: unrelated classes sharing a capability vs a real family of related classes sharing code.

This topic covers the practical decision between them, how default methods blurred the historical line, and where a too-broad interface causes real design pain.

slides.sectionTitle: Interface vs abstract class: contract-only vs partial implementation
slides.markdown:
An **interface** declares what a class can do, with historically zero implementation — `interface Flyable { void fly(); }` says nothing about how flying happens, only that it must be possible. An **abstract class** can go further: it can implement some methods fully, shared by every subclass, while leaving others `abstract` for subclasses to fill in — `abstract class Bird { void breathe() {...}; abstract void fly(); }` gives every bird the same breathing logic for free.

The practical difference is about shared code, not just terminology: reach for an interface when unrelated classes need to satisfy the same contract with entirely different internals (a `Bird` and a `Plane` can both `Flyable`, sharing nothing else); reach for an abstract class when a real family of related classes shares actual implementation, not just a method name.

slides.sectionTitle: Multiple interface implementation vs single-class inheritance
slides.markdown:
A class can implement as many interfaces as it needs — `class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable, Quackable` is completely legal — but can extend at most one abstract (or concrete) class in languages like Java and C#. This asymmetry is deliberate: interfaces carry no state, so there's no diamond-problem ambiguity about which parent's fields win; abstract classes can carry state and partial implementation, which is exactly what makes combining several of them ambiguous.

This is what makes interfaces the right tool for capabilities that cut across unrelated class families — `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Flyable` — where a class might need several such capabilities at once, but only ever has one "real" place in a class hierarchy, if it has one at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Default/static methods on interfaces — how modern languages blurred the line
slides.markdown:
Java 8+ (and similar features in C#, Kotlin) added **default methods** to interfaces — a method with a real body, that implementing classes inherit automatically unless they choose to override it. `interface Flyable { default void fly() { System.out.println("flap flap"); } }` gives every `Flyable` a working `fly()` for free, something only abstract classes could historically do.

This was added specifically to solve a real evolution problem: adding a new method to a widely-implemented interface used to break every existing implementer, since they'd suddenly be missing a required method. A default method lets the interface grow without breaking anyone — existing implementers just inherit the default.

The line hasn't fully disappeared, though: interfaces still can't hold instance state (fields), only behavior, so an abstract class remains the right tool the moment shared *state* — not just shared behavior — is what a family of classes needs.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: interface vs abstract class inside the same hierarchy
slides.markdown:
A realistic hierarchy often uses both at once: `Comparable` (an interface) sits alongside `AbstractShape` (an abstract class) as two separate things a concrete `Circle` depends on. `AbstractShape` provides shared implementation every shape needs (like a cached `toString()`), plus one `abstract area()` method subclasses must fill in. `Comparable` is a cross-cutting capability — `Circle implements Comparable<Circle>` — unrelated to the shape hierarchy itself, just a contract `Circle` also happens to satisfy.

`Circle` ends up extending exactly one class (`AbstractShape`) while implementing as many interfaces as it needs (`Comparable`, possibly `Serializable` too) — the asymmetry from the previous slide, visible in one concrete class.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: when to use an interface vs an abstract class
slides.markdown:
A practical decision table, not just a feature comparison:

| Situation | Choose |
|---|---|
| Unrelated classes need the same capability, no shared code | Interface |
| A class needs multiple unrelated capabilities at once | Interface (multiple implementable) |
| A real family of related classes shares actual field state | Abstract class |
| Some methods should have one shared default implementation | Either (default methods) or abstract class if state is involved |
| You're not sure yet, and want maximum flexibility later | Interface — easier to add an abstract class alongside later than to remove one |

**How to decide fast:** ask "does this need shared *state*, not just shared *behavior*?" State pushes you toward an abstract class; behavior-only, especially behavior needed across unrelated types, pushes you toward an interface.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: the same small design done both ways
Pitfall: a fat interface that forces classes to implement methods they don't need
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll put every method a `Worker` might ever need on one `Worker` interface, so any implementer has the full capability set available."

**Why it's wrong:** a `Worker` interface with `code()`, `attendMeetings()`, and `fileReports()` forces a class like `RobotWorker`, which genuinely can't `attendMeetings()`, to either implement a meaningless method (throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`, or silently doing nothing) or fake compliance with the contract. Either way, callers relying on the interface can no longer trust that every method actually works for every implementer — the contract has quietly become a lie for some types.

**Correct model:** split fat interfaces into focused ones — `Codeable`, `MeetingAttendee`, `ReportFiler` — so a class implements only the capabilities it genuinely has, and every method on every interface it implements actually works. This is the Interface Segregation Principle, covered as its own topic — this is the exact problem it exists to prevent.

slides.sectionTitle: Marker interfaces and their modern replacements (annotations/attributes)
slides.markdown:
A **marker interface** has zero methods — it exists purely so `instanceof` or reflection can check "does this class opt into some behavior?" Java's `Serializable` is the classic example: implementing it adds no methods to write, but tells the serialization framework this class is safe to convert to bytes.

Modern languages mostly replaced this pattern with **annotations** (Java `@Deprecated`, C# attributes) — `@Serializable` conveys the same opt-in signal without occupying a class's one `extends`/limited `implements` slot with something that adds no real contract, and annotations can also carry parameters (`@Retention(RUNTIME)`) that a method-less interface never could.

The interview-relevant point: marker interfaces still exist in older APIs (`Serializable`, `Cloneable`) and you should recognize the pattern, but new designs almost always reach for an annotation instead — it's a strictly more expressive tool for the same "tag this class" job.
